title: It was never whale vomit
whisper: the grey amber that floats for years
renderedWith: raea/sillage-006-ambergris (map fields unused; this file holds the script and the voice)

beats.say: Fishermen in Yemen found {127|a hundred and twenty-seven} kilos of whale vomit. It sold for {$1.5 million|one point five million dollars}.
One problem. It was never vomit.
It's ambergris. Old French for grey amber.
It forms in the intestine of a sperm whale, from a secretion of the bile duct. Hard squid beaks are often found inside.
And it mostly leaves the other way. Like dung.
Only about one sperm whale in a hundred makes it. Old Soviet whaling logs found even fewer.
Fresh, it smells like what it is. Then it floats at sea, often for years.
Slowly, it turns sweet and earthy.
The secret is chemistry. A scentless molecule, ambrein, breaks down into ambroxide. That is the smell.
Egyptians burned it as incense. People carried balls of it against the plague. Eggs with ambergris were reportedly a favourite of King Charles the Second.
Today, owning it is illegal in the United States. In Britain and the E U, it can be sold.
That piece from Yemen? About {$12|twelve dollars} a gram.
So perfumers found a shortcut. Ambroxide is now made from clary sage. A plant.
But the headlines never change. They still say:

creative.thesis: The headline word (vomit) is wrong; the record says gut, dung, chemistry.
creative.opening: hold on the grey lump on a plinth with the price

creative.payoff: the bottle fills grey on 'That is the smell'
